figures.caption: Overview of DreamRealm. Top: RealmForgePipe mines hallucinated responses through high-temperature sampling and key-attribute enumeration, selects candidates through likelihood ranking and Top-K filtering, and edits images to make the selected hallucinated responses valid. Bottom: RealmMatch constructs an image–response score matrix from original images with their ground-truth answers and edited images with their corresponding hallucinated responses. Through SFT on matched image–response pairs and bidirectional contrastive learning, it assigns hallucinated responses to their supporting images, learning the correspondence between responses and visual conditions.

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model’s own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image–response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

sections.body: Post-training methods either correct responses under a fixed image or build visual contrasts without targeting the model's own confusions. DreamRealm instead explores latent hallucinated responses through repeated high-temperature sampling and enumeration of key attributes, minimally edits original images so that selected responses become valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. On Qwen3.5-9B, the paper reports gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy across six benchmarks. The motivation is a human analogy: correcting a child who mistakes medicine for candy also involves showing what real candy looks like.
sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.headline: Visual hallucinations persist, and existing post-training rarely builds supervision around the model's own perceptual confusions.

sections.body: Hallucination-aware fine-tuning methods such as HALVA, RLAIF-V, REVERSE and FINER correct or contrast responses while keeping the image fixed. Visual-contrast methods such as SymMPO and CoCI build contrasts from retrieved real images, while IC-VCO and MED build them through generated or edited images. VCD applies visual contrast at inference time. The authors state that these visual contrasts are not designed around the target model's hallucinations. DreamRealm differs in two ways: it learns to assign diverse latent hallucinated responses to supporting visual conditions, and it derives its editing targets from the target model's own hallucinations.
sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work corrects responses under fixed images or builds visual contrasts from retrieved or generated images, not from the target model's hallucinations.

sections.body: RealmForgePipe has two stages. Hallucination exploration samples responses at a high temperature, adds enumerated attribute values, removes semantic duplicates, scores candidates by mean token log-likelihood, and keeps the top `K_mine` candidates. Hallucination materialization asks a verifier MLLM for three edit instructions ordered by expected edit extent. An image model tries them in order, and an edit is accepted only if the minimal-editing score is at least 4/5 and a blind check confirms the target response. RealmMatch then fills a score matrix over original and edited images and applies row-wise and column-wise contrastive losses, with SFT on matched pairs. RealmSet contains 28,960 human-approved edited examples across 22 categories.
sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.headline: RealmForgePipe mines and edits hallucinations, and RealmMatch trains a likelihood matrix with bidirectional contrastive losses to assign responses to images.

sections.body: The authors train Qwen3.5-9B with RealmMatch on RealmSet and compare it with the raw checkpoint and several specialized hallucination-mitigation methods under one evaluation protocol. On Qwen3.5-9B, DreamRealm improves all seven metrics and is best on six. ObjectHal is the exception, where it stays close to the best result from RLAIF-V. The same RealmSet used to train Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-4-E4B-it and InternVL3.5-8B improves most metrics, but by less than in the matched setting, and Gemma and InternVL regress slightly on CV-Bench-2D. In ablations, original-only supervision degrades HallusionBench, adding latent hallucinations improves all seven metrics over observed-only data, and SFT alone is best on AMBER.
sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.headline: DreamRealm improves all seven Qwen3.5-9B metrics, and ablations show latent hallucinations add gains beyond observed errors.

sections.body: The authors state that DreamRealm incurs data construction costs, including image generation with GPT-Image and human review, detailed in Appendices D and D.2. Because the method depends on the capabilities of the underlying image-editing model, some scenes remain difficult to edit successfully. Appendix D.1 reports the final pass rates of RealmForgePipe across 22 question categories, measured as the share of synthesis candidates ultimately approved by human review.
sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.headline: Data construction is costly, and the image-editing model's limits leave some scenes hard to edit.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the framework: DreamRealm materializes a model's hallucination world and uses contrastive learning to assign hallucinated responses to their corresponding visual inputs. The authors cite consistent improvements across multiple benchmarks as evidence of the approach's potential to enhance visual perception and mitigate visual hallucinations. The section adds no new experiments and does not restate the limitations given in Section 5.
sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.headline: Authors conclude that hallucination assignment shows potential to improve visual perception and mitigate hallucinations across benchmarks.

sections.body: This appendix gives the full editing algorithm, with three verifier scores, a limit of two synthesis attempts per instruction-type pair, and strict, relaxed and skip blind-check modes. Human annotators review each candidate before curation. It also includes mining and editing examples, data construction counts in Table 1, category-wise pass rates in Table 2, a worked editing trace, training settings with Table 3 hyperparameters, and qualitative comparisons. Human review used 12 annotators, a second quality check on 10% of the data, and a throughput of 500 samples per annotator-hour.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists the editing algorithm, mining and editing examples, category statistics, annotation protocol, a worked example, training settings, and qualitative comparisons.
